notes:
I found sources for most of the chapter's main questions, but not for every verse or every tradition. The gaps are listed at the end. Most points are in my own words; quoted phrases are short. "Futurist" means reading most of the chapter as still to come before Christ's return. "AD 70" means the Roman destruction of Jerusalem and the temple.

**v. 1**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): the disciples were like amazed tourists. Herod's rebuilt temple was one of the great buildings of the ancient world, but for many Jews it had become a kind of idol. Jesus said He was greater than the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/
- Constable: the stones the disciple pointed to were probably the temple buildings and porches, not the foundation stones. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 2**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: Titus ordered the whole city and temple to be demolished, according to Josephus. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Mar/Mar_013.cfm
- Guzik: because this prophecy came true literally, the other prophecies in the chapter should be expected to come true literally too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/
- Constable: AD 70 fulfilled it, but not completely, since foundation stones still stand. He thinks full fulfilment waits for the future Tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 3–4**
- Wesley (Methodist): two questions are here asked; the one concerning the destruction of Jerusalem: the other concerning the end of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Constable: the disciples assumed the temple's fall and the end of the age would happen together. Jesus taught that they would not. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html
- Sproul (Reformed): the temple's fall, Jerusalem's fall and Christ's coming are all included in "all these things." https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-olivet-discourse-part-2

**v. 5–6**
- Constable: "take heed" comes four times in the chapter, so warning is a main theme. "I am He" echoes God's own name, so these false messiahs claim to be God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html
- Guzik: they will pretend to be Jesus, or to speak for Him, but they do not truly represent Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/

**v. 7–8**
- Guzik: wars, famines and earthquakes are not signs of the end. "Birth pains" points to a new age being born, perhaps with troubles growing stronger and more frequent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/
- Constable (futurist): these things run through the whole present age and also mark the first half of the future Tribulation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 9**
- Constable: persecution will come from both Jewish and Gentile courts, religious and secular, and it becomes a chance to bear witness. The warning applies to disciples in every age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 10**
- Constable: "must" means God has decreed it. He argues the verse is not a promise that preaching will bring in the kingdom, which he says is the postmillennial view. It also does not mean everyone will believe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html
- Guzik: persecution does not excuse the church from this task. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/

**v. 11**
- Guzik: Acts 4 is an example. He quotes A.T. Robertson: the promise is about moments of persecution and is no excuse for preachers who skip preparing their sermons. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/
- Wesley: The Holy Ghost will help you. But do not depend upon any other help For all the nearest ties will be broken. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm

**v. 12–13**
- Guzik: the Greek word for "endure" means to "remain under." In trials, believers should not grab at an escape that means compromise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/
- Constable: faithful endurance brings deliverance, whether in this life, at death, or at Christ's return. He notes that not all disciples endure. Even so, final salvation rests on God's faithfulness to keep believers, not on how well they endure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 14** (the most debated verse)
- Futurist (Guzik): Antiochus Epiphanes' desecration of the temple before Christ only foreshadowed this. It is a still-future idol in a rebuilt temple, which he links to 2 Thessalonians 2. He cites Irenaeus as an early witness for this view. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/
- Constable: he sees three layers: Antiochus in the past, the temple's pollution before AD 70, and the Antichrist still to come. Mark pairs a neuter noun with a masculine verb, which suggests the abomination is a person. Christians fleeing to Pella foreshadowed a future flight. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html
- AD 70 reading (Benson, on Bible Hub): the abomination signifies the Roman armies, with their standards, whereon the images of their idols were painted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-14.htm
- H.B. Charles Jr. (Baptist pastor): he names both views. Some faithful teachers see AD 70 here, when Titus desecrated the temple, but he holds that the Antichrist will commit the abomination of desolation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/charles_hb/sermons/mark/the-abomination-of-desolation-mark-13-v14-23.cfm
- "Let the reader understand": GotQuestions says this may be Mark's note, or Jesus telling readers of Daniel to understand. https://www.gotquestions.org/let-the-reader-understand.html
- Ellicott: Mark's riddle-like "where it should not be" is probably closer to what Jesus actually said than Matthew's "holy place." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-14.htm

**v. 15–18**
- Constable: the point is that flight must be immediate and urgent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 19**
- Wesley asks whether this has been fully accomplished yet: Is not much of this affliction still to come? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Constable: Jesus looks past AD 70 to a much greater Tribulation. Guzik links it to the time of wrath in Revelation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 20**
- Wesley: "the elect" are Christians, set apart from the world through the Spirit's sanctifying work and belief in the truth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Constable (dispensational): God has already limited the Tribulation to seven years, based on Daniel 9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 21–23**
- Constable: "if that were possible" does not mean the elect will certainly hold firm, or Jesus' warnings would be pointless. It describes what the deceivers intend. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html This touches the debate over whether true believers always persevere, but I found no Reformed source on this verse to set beside him.

**v. 24–25**
- Wesley: these are the days just before the end of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Constable: these signs should be taken literally. They describe the Second Coming, not the Rapture. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html
- Matthew Henry: Christ corrected the disciples' mistake of merging Jerusalem's fall with the end, and here foretells the final dissolution of the present frame and fabric of the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-26.htm

**v. 26**
- Background: MacArthur (gty.org, Baptist) traces the verse to Daniel 7:13, Christ receiving His kingdom. https://www.gty.org/sermons/41-68/coming-in-the-clouds
- Ligonier (Reformed): this verse shows "Son of Man" cannot refer only to Jesus' humanity. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/he-who-comes-clouds
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the verse finds its highest meaning in the Second Coming, but asks whether that be the primary sense of it as it stands here? It points to Daniel 7 as the key. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-26.htm
- Catholic (Jimmy Akin): this may point to the Second Coming, but in context it refers to Jesus coming spiritually as judge on the temple in AD 70. The imagery echoes God "riding the clouds" in the Old Testament. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/jesus-botched-predicting-the-end-times

**v. 27**
- Akin (Catholic): Christ, now given dominion, gathers His elect through the spread of the gospel. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/jesus-botched-predicting-the-end-times
- Constable: all believers, living and dead, gather to Christ at His return. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 28–29**
- Wesley: "He is nigh" means the Son of Man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Constable: the lesson is that alert people can read signs before an event happens. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 30** (the second big dispute)
- Futurist (Guzik): it cannot mean the disciples' generation, because they did not see Jesus return. It means the generation that sees the signs, especially the abomination. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/mark-13/ Guzik also allows that "generation" could mean the Jewish race. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/mark/mark-13.cfm
- Constable: fulfilment began in the disciples' generation and is completed later, or "generation" means the Jewish race. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html
- Reformed (Sproul): he rejects stretched redefinitions of "generation," which he calls frankly torturous. He insists that in some sense Jesus did come at the end of that forty-year period, while also weighing a near-and-far fulfilment. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-olivet-discourse-part-2 and https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/mark-christ-coming-glory
- Methodist (Wesley): "all these things" means relating to the temple and the city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Catholic (Akin): the verse refers to the events leading up to AD 70. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/jesus-botched-predicting-the-end-times
- Bible Hub summary: Irenaeus read verse 30 as meaning the final generation. https://biblehub.com/q/Scholars_view_on_Mark_13_30_timing.htm

**v. 31**
- Constable: "heaven and earth" means all creation. By putting His words above the universe, Jesus implies that He is God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**v. 32** (the problem of "nor the Son")
- Wesley: Not as man: as man he was no more omniscient than omnipresent. But as God he knows all the circumstances of it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- Gill (Baptist): the Son knew it as God but not as man. Gill applies the verse to the day of judgment on the Jews. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/mark/13-32.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the answer lies in the union of Christ's two natures. As man and messenger, He did not know it in a way He could reveal. https://biblehub.com/mark/13-32.htm
- Ellicott: he rejects readings that explain the words away. He sees a real, self-chosen limitation, linked to Christ "emptying Himself" in Philippians 2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-32.htm
- Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): don't pry curiously into the date; take care that it doesn't catch you unprepared. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-32.htm
- Utley: the phrase is missing from some ancient manuscripts but present in the strongest ones. https://bible.org/seriespage/mark-13

**v. 33–37**
- Wesley: Christ assigns duties to all His servants. The parable "seems chiefly" to concern ministers at the day of judgment, but can apply to everyone and to the time of death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/mark/13.htm
- A sermon on Bible Hub applies the call to watch to each person's own last day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mark/13-32.htm
- Constable (pretribulational): believers watch because the Rapture could come at any moment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/mark-13.html

**What I couldn't find (so left out):**
- Lutheran sources (lcms.org, 1517.org).
- Orthodox sources (oca.org).
- Modern scholarship from bibleodyssey.org or the netbible.org notes.
- Any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- A Pentecostal source other than Guzik.
- A Reformed source on perseverance for verses 13 and 22.
- Notes for verses 15–18 and 28–29 that go beyond the brief ones above.

The Enduring Word page I read also stopped partway through verse 14, so Guzik's notes on verses 15–37 come only from search excerpts.
